Skip next section Germany to send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine 09/08/2026 September 8, 2026 Germany to send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius says Berlin will provide Ukraine with additional interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks as Kyiv seeks to bolster its defenses against Russian aerial attacks. "I decided to deliver urgently needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine," Pistorius told a video meeting of defense ministers from countries supporting Kyiv. He also urged other Ukraine backers to examine their own inventories and consider similar deliveries. Pistorius said Germany would also increase supplies of air-to-air missiles and continue providing drones and long-range ammunition to Ukraine. Separately, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Kyiv was contracting the supply of around 1,000 missiles for US-designed Patriot systems with help from allies and through a European Union loan. Khmara said most of those missiles would only be delivered in the coming years and called for more immediate assistance. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Illustration: Anna Ivanenko/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Anna Ivanenko/The Guardian Opinion Ukraine Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back Anna Ivanenko Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Share Sometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”. For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury. Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours after US Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow . Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time. I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time. https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/world-n.text: A man accused of killing his girlfriend and stuffing her body into a suitcase before dumping it in a river has been arrested a 700 miles form where she was found. Hairstylist Valentina Tănăsie, 28, was found dead inside a suitcase floating near the bank of the Olt River in Romania. After an extensive manhunt, her boyfriend Vlad Bălțățeanu, 30, was charged with her murder. Police say he fled the country before he could be arrested before surrendering to officers in Switzerland. Valentina and Bălțățeanu are believed to have argued on the night of 20 September after he accused her of cheating on him – a claim she denied - with them both having had a few drinks. Valentina’s father reported her missing the following day after she failed to answer his calls. On 22 September, fishermen spotted a suitcase floating near the bank of the Olt River. Valentina’s naked body was discovered inside. Forensic doctors found two traumatic injuries to her head and five broken ribs, as well as abrasions and wounds to her lower legs. They concluded she had died on 21 September from traumatic and haemorrhagic shock. Adrian Vrăbete, a spokesman for Vâlcea’s prosecutor’s office, said: “The injuries were found to have been caused by blows with hard objects, an object with a pointed and sharp edge, possibly a knife, and compression of the chest and abdomen, possibly by someone sitting on the victim.” Investigators searched Bălțățeanu’s home in Tomşani on 23 September. Vrăbete said officers discovered “multiple reddish-brown stains that appear to be blood” on a mattress inside the property. Bălțățeanu, who is originally from Horezu, was charged with murder. However, he allegedly crossed the Romanian border into Hungary before he could be arrested and Romanian media now report that he surrendered more than 700 miles from the scene. Bălțățeanu reportedly walked into a police station in St Gallen, Switzerland, on Monday night (28 Sep) and allegedly admitted killing Valentina. Investigators believe he initially travelled to Hungary in a friend’s car before continuing towards Italy in a minibus and completing the journey to Switzerland by train. He is now in the custody of Swiss authorities, with proceedings expected to begin to return him to Romania. Valentina and Bălțățeanu had reportedly met online and been in a relationship for around three months. Local reports claim their relationship had been marked by violent arguments and jealousy. Valentina, who was originally from Dolj County, “wanted to get pregnant and start a family”, an uncle told local media following her death. Romanian media have also reported that a 17-year-old girl made allegations against Bălțățeanu in September 2022. She reportedly accused him of assaulting her, holding her captive at his home and raping her. Several other women who reportedly dated Bălțățeanu have since spoken publicly about alleged episodes of jealousy and aggression, with one said to have obtained a restraining order. Lawyer Adrian Cuculis, who is representing Valentina’s family, told Romanian media: “There’s no way he’ll get any reduction in his sentence for turning himself in and admitting to the crime. “He’ll probably get life, given that it’s a femicide.”
